Locks nothing: it only says where each module starts. A task that works without the board starts without it, and the session summary is spoken instead of shown — otherwise a screen you are not looking at would be waiting for you at the end. You still choose the support on the module page, and the plan moves it for you as you go.
How you say squares into the microphone. Everything is in English.
The file is said as a word: “bravo” instead of “b”. Helps when the model confuses similar letters. The words are the ones pilots and radio operators use.
The words are English and only the English package recognises them. If a square is not getting through, try this.
Say the whole move at once

The move is said in one breath — “e four e two” — instead of one press per square. A pause is fine: the microphone waits for the second square. Applies only to Convert the Win, the one exercise where the answer is a move and not a single square.

In Convert the Win you may also say “rook e two” — the starting square is found for you. Works alongside saying squares, nothing to choose. When two identical pieces can reach the same square, the app says so and asks for the starting square.
You may say “e”, then “four”, instead of the whole square at once.
You know a square’s colour and place at once, without counting.
From a given square you see at once where the piece can go.
You hold where each piece stands, with nothing leaking away.
You apply a move without spoiling the picture. This is where it most often falls apart.
You hear “g1 f3” and see it; and the other way round.
You notice the picture has fallen apart and put it back together.
You know what the opponent guards and which square is hot.
You follow a line without a board.
A skill with no data yet. That is not a weakness — it is simply not known yet.
How much you have put in, not how far you have got. Points and rank measure time and persistence; how far you have got is in Progress, for each skill separately.

Why blindfold, what the skills are and how they are measured.
About a minute, always the same, no points — so it can be compared with the last time.

If you have to count to know that e4 is a light square, you know the right answer and still lack the skill. What is measured here is not whether you know, but what it costs you. It fails quietly: everything is correct, only everything else falls apart, because attention that is counting squares is not holding the position.

From a given square you see at once how far the piece reaches — without listing square by square. The knight is the boundary: with the knight it shows most clearly whether you really see the reach or work it out afresh every time. It fails by every move taking a moment too long.

The piece–square links stay stable while you move nothing. It fails by leaking, not by collapsing: a piece quietly vanishes from the picture and you do not notice — because if you had noticed, you would have put it back. That is why what is measured is how many you can hold, not whether you know them.

This is the bottleneck, not holding. A static position is remembered fairly easily; the picture spoils on change, because every move brings a new chance for something to drop out, and mistakes do not cancel out but pile up. It fails by the first ten moves going perfectly and then, suddenly, nothing standing.

You hear “g1 f3” and see the move, with no step in between; and the other way round, you can say what you see. While that translation is conscious, everything you listen to runs slower than the game. It fails on the opponent’s moves before your own.

First you notice that the picture has fallen apart, then you put it back together. Without this, after the first mistake the guessing continues, because admitting to yourself that you no longer know where the rook is feels like a loss — and it is not; it is the only moment when the game can still be saved.

In a real blindfold game pieces are not lost because you forget where they stand, but because you forget what they guard. Holding the position tells you the bishop is on g7; square control tells you that because of it you must not go to d4. It fails as a move that is simply hanging.

You follow a line without a board — that is, you change the picture several times and bring it back to the start. It demands everything before it at once, and that is why it comes last: while updating or square control are eating attention, calculation has nothing to work with.

This app does not teach you chess. It teaches you to hold it in your head.

Blindfold play does not break down because you do not know what a good move is, but because by move twelve you no longer know where the bishop is. That is not one flaw of memory but a set of habits that are trained separately — and that, until trained, choke each other, because they all happen in the same head at the same time.

That is why there is no single “play blindfold” exercise here. There are several, kept apart, and each is practised on its own.

Next to each one: what it means, what it looks like when it fails, and what trains it in the app. What trains it is not copied in by hand — it is read from the tasks themselves, so it is always accurate.
No task measures it for now — it rides along with the others.
No check-up — how much you have practised is known, your level is not.
How they rest on one another

The reason is not pedagogical but mechanical: there is one working memory. If finding the square e4 eats attention, there is nothing left to hold the position with — so holding does not improve however much you practise it.

Automatic does not mean correct. It means fast, without thinking: a correct answer that cost you three seconds is still spending attention that should be doing something else.

A prerequisite locks nothing. It enters only the suggestion and this picture. If the estimate is wrong, you are still standing in front of an open door.

Some skills in the picture have no continuation — nothing rests on them. That does not make them superfluous; it makes them something other than a foundation, and they matter for a different reason.

NOTATION TO PICTURE is the entrance. Blindfold, the game reaches you only as notation — “knight g one f three” — so while that is being translated consciously, there is nothing to update yet. You fall behind the opponent not because of the picture but because of the decoding. The app does not require it as a foundation, because its tasks give you the move both spoken and written; at a board without a board it is the only entrance you have.

PICTURE RECOVERY is insurance. Everything else carries you through the game while it goes well; recovery decides what happens when it goes badly. Without it, the first mistake ends the game — from there on it is guessing, because admitting to yourself that you no longer know where the rook is feels like a loss, and it is the only moment when the game can still be saved. That is also why the depth to the first mistake is measured: it says how long the picture holds, and recovery is the only thing that decides what happens after that point.

BLINDFOLD CALCULATION has no continuation for a third reason — it is the top. Everything else leads to it.
Why a plan, not just practice

Practise what the app suggests, not what first comes to mind. The reason is not discipline but that both first thoughts are wrong.

The first is to do what you are good at. That is pleasant and moves nothing — a skill that is already automatic does not become more automatic.

The second is to do what looks most like the real thing: a whole game blindfold. That is the fastest way to give up. A game demands every skill at once, so when it collapses you do not know which one gave way. You practise everything and fix nothing.

That is why you work from the bottom up, and why the order is not a matter of taste.

An exercise that merely carries a skill does not build it. “Follow the Game” uses coordinates on every move, but if your coordinates are not automatic, that is not where you will build them — it is where you will keep falling because of them. It is fixed below and used above.

And one more thing that is easy to overlook: when a skill is measured on its own, that number is better than it will be in a game. A square’s colour in three seconds was measured while you were doing nothing else. The same job while you are holding five pieces in your head is not the same job.

That is why what is measured here is not only whether you know, but also what it costs you.

This can be practised with your eyes closed, lying down, with the phone in your hand or beside you.

That is why there are two ways of working. While you look at the screen, there are the board and the buttons. While you do not, the screen splits into a few large zones: the finger is not aimed but simply put down, each zone vibrates differently, and the layout is the same in every module — so the hand learns it once and knows it everywhere. The question is heard, and you answer by voice or by touch.

You choose the way of working in Settings, once for all modules.

This is not a convenience but half the reason this app exists. Blindfold chess is played without a board in front of you — an exercise that requires you to look at the screen teaches you something you will not need in a game. And the time in which you can practise like this, on the bus or before sleep, would otherwise not be used for anything.

Not every module works this way, and the row says so. “Remember the Position” and “Set Up by Dictation” need the board, because the pieces are put back on their squares.

Three things that are easy to mix up and mean different things.

A MODULE is a tool — a row on the Train tab. “Follow the Game”, “Give Check”.

A TASK is what is actually measured. The same module can ask things that do not measure the same skill: “where is the knight now” measures updating the picture, while “who attacks the knight” measures square control. Same input, different skill. That is why a module with two tasks has a “Task” row on its page — it starts on the one you did last time.

SUPPORT is how much of the picture the app holds for you, and that is the real difficulty of blindfold practice. EASY / MEDIUM / HARD changes how much there is and how fast — that is effort. Support changes how much you have to hold yourself.

Less support means harder. It is the only scale here that runs that way, so it is worth remembering.
What support means exactly depends on the task, and the task says so on its screen. Only the order is shared — from the most support to the least.
The board is visible the whole time. Reading and speed are practised, not holding.

The board is visible until you say you have memorised it, then part of the picture disappears. The boundary is your confirmation, not a clock: with the pieces in front of your eyes the exercise shrinks to reading, and the picture in your head never gets built.
Only traces remain — squares without pieces.
Nothing is shown. The position is heard, and you answer by voice or by the screen zones.

The same exercise with less support measures a different skill. “Give Check” with the board is reading lines; the same task after “I HAVE MEMORISED IT” is square control from memory. That is why support enters the grade, and in the profile it counts for more than the accuracy percentage.

For every support level of every task there is a benchmark — both time and accuracy. A pair, not a number: if only time stood there, the measure would invite haste, and haste brings accuracy down, which is half the skill. It is credited only when both are met.

The benchmark is not a ceiling and may be passed. Once you pass it, it stops being the horizon and becomes the floor — the benchmark of the next, lower support level takes over.

AUTOMATIC is a skill that holds its support level and is noticeably faster than the benchmark there — roughly a quarter below it. It is measured against the benchmark of that task, because an attempt is in one place a three-second question and in another a whole position of a minute and a half; one and the same number of seconds for all would mean that some skills are never credited.

DEPTH TO THE FIRST MISTAKE is the most useful number here, and accuracy does not tell it. Seventy per cent accuracy does not say what a game looks like: one person makes mistakes evenly, another’s picture falls apart on move six and from there on they guess at random. The first is fixed by practice; the second is the limit of what the head currently holds. The first mistake is what is kept, because after it the picture is already spoiled, so the remaining answers do not measure the same thing.

“Not measured” is not zero. Zero would say you are bad at it; the truth is that nothing is known about it yet. That is why the empty places in the profile say exactly that.

Practice tells you how you are progressing in that task. It does not tell you your level, because you chose the difficulty, the support and how many times to repeat.

A check-up is therefore always the same: the same task, the same difficulty, the same number of questions. It is the only measurement that may be compared with last month.

It earns no points, and that is said before you start it, not after. A measure that rewards stops measuring — the moment a check-up gave points, it would be done for the points.

A check-up does not exist for every skill. For the others, how much you have practised is known, but not where you stand, and that is written next to each skill instead of being left unsaid.

What to do now: which skill, with which task, with how much support — and why that one.

The reason is not decoration. A recommendation without a reason is a prophecy, and a prophecy is not trusted once it misses; with a reason it is an argument, and you are allowed to disagree.

How it chooses, in order:

1. Never the same thing twice in a row — a plateau is not broken by repetition, and the other skills wither in the meantime.
2. Now and then, what you are good at. A recommendation that always sends you to the worst place is a recommendation that stops being opened.
3. Foundation before what is built on it.
4. Untried before weak — nothing is known about the untried, and that is worth more than one more confirmation that something is weak.
5. Otherwise, the weakest.

It chooses the support from the last time: twice in a row successful at the same support and next time you get less of it; a miss brings it back, with no penalty and no comment.

Nothing is locked. The list of modules stays untouched below the card, declining has no consequences, and rank opens nothing. If you do not feel like doing what is suggested, do not.
The list is the same one as on the Train tab. Next to each module: which tasks it carries and how much support it can do.
No session has been measured by skill yet. Do one exercise and come back.
Sessions done before skills were introduced have no breakdown and do not enter the profile.
